subproblems.title: Structure of degree-0 integer multiplicity triples (reused accepted lemma)
subproblems.lean_statement: ∀ (P : ℕ) (U : Set (Euclid P)) (R : IMRep U 0), R.carrier.Countable ∧ (∀ K : Set (Euclid P), IsCompact K → K ⊆ U → (R.carrier ∩ K).Finite ∧ R.measure K ≠ ∞) ∧ (∀ x ∈ R.carrier, (∃ Q : Submodule ℝ (Euclid P), HasApproximateTangentSpaceAt 0 R.carrier x Q ∧ IsUnitOrientationOf (R.orient x) Q) ∧ R.orient x ≠ 0) ∧ (IsOpen U → U ∩ R.measure.support = R.carrier)
subproblems.natural_proof:
Source: steps 1, 2, 4 and 5 of the parent proof, stated for an arbitrary domain U. Those steps show:
- H⁰ = μH[0] gives every point mass 1;
- a carrier point x has μ_R({x}) = θ(x) ≥ 1;
- local integrability of θ ≥ 1 forces the carrier to be locally finite;
- singletons of positive H⁰-mass upgrade the a.e. orientation condition to every carrier point.
The remaining conjuncts are proved in full below: countability, μ_R(K) ≠ ∞, ξ(x) ≠ 0, and U ∩ spt μ_R ⊆ M. Simon uses H⁰ = counting measure (chapter-02.txt line 787) and defines (M, θ, ξ) in Ch. 6, 3.1 (chapter-06.txt lines 733–753). Notation: M = R.carrier, θ = R.mult, ξ = R.orient, H⁰ = μHE[0], μ_R = R.measure = (H⁰⌞M).withDensity θ.

1. Facts about H⁰.
   - H⁰ = μH[0] (Measure.euclideanHausdorffMeasure_zero).
   - Hence H⁰({z}) = 1 for every z ∈ ℝ^P (Measure.hausdorffMeasure_zero_singleton).
   - By monotonicity, H⁰(A) ≥ H⁰({z}) = 1 for every set A containing a point z.
   - Singletons are Borel, so H⁰(t) = Σ_{z∈t} H⁰({z}) = #t for every finite set t (sum_measure_singleton).
   - Compact subsets of ℝ^P are closed, hence Borel.

2. (i) M is countable.
   - The field R.rectifiable (CountablyRectifiable 0 M) gives M₀ ⊆ ℝ^P with H⁰(M₀) = 0, and maps F_j : ℝ⁰ → ℝ^P (j ∈ ℕ) with M ⊆ M₀ ∪ ⋃_j range F_j.
   - If M₀ were nonempty, step 1 would give H⁰(M₀) ≥ 1. Hence M₀ = ∅.
   - The domain ℝ⁰ = EuclideanSpace ℝ (Fin 0) has exactly one point: two functions on the empty index type Fin 0 are equal by function extensionality. So each range F_j has at most one point.
   - Thus M lies in a countable union of sets with at most one point, so M is countable.

3. (ii) Let K ⊆ U be compact, hence Borel.
   - By withDensity_apply and Measure.restrict_restrict, μ_R(K) = ∫⁻_K θ d(H⁰⌞M) = ∫⁻_{M∩K} θ dH⁰ =: I.
   - I ≠ ∞ by the field R.locallyIntegrable_mult applied to K (IsCompact K, K ⊆ U). So μ_R(K) ≠ ∞.
   - θ is ℕ-valued with θ > 0 on M (R.mult_pos), so θ ≥ 1 on M. Since M ∩ K is Borel, H⁰(M ∩ K) = ∫⁻_{M∩K} 1 dH⁰ ≤ I < ∞ (setLIntegral_mono').
   - Suppose M ∩ K were infinite. For every m ∈ ℕ it contains a finite set t with #t = m (Set.Infinite.exists_subset_card_eq). By step 1 and monotonicity, m = H⁰(t) ≤ H⁰(M ∩ K).
   - Since m is arbitrary, H⁰(M ∩ K) = ∞, a contradiction. Hence M ∩ K is finite.

4. (iii) Let p(z) be the property "∃ Q, HasApproximateTangentSpaceAt 0 M z Q ∧ IsUnitOrientationOf (ξ(z)) Q".
   - The field R.orients says p holds (H⁰⌞M)-a.e., i.e. (H⁰⌞M)(N) = 0 for N := {z : ¬p(z)} (ae_iff).
   - Suppose some x ∈ M fails p. Then {x} ⊆ N.
   - Since {x} is Borel and x ∈ M, (H⁰⌞M)({x}) = H⁰({x} ∩ M) = H⁰({x}) = 1 (Measure.restrict_apply).
   - Monotonicity gives 1 ≤ (H⁰⌞M)(N) = 0, a contradiction. Hence p(x) holds for every x ∈ M.
   - Now fix x ∈ M and take Q and τ : Fin 0 → ℝ^P from IsUnitOrientationOf (ξ(x)) Q. Then either ξ(x)(α) = α(τ) for every 0-covector α, or ξ(x)(α) = −α(τ) for every α.
   - Let α₁ be the constant 0-covector with value 1 (ContinuousAlternatingMap.constOfIsEmpty ℝ (Euclid P) (Fin 0) 1), so α₁(τ) = 1.
   - Then ξ(x)(α₁) = ±1. If ξ(x) were 0 this would read 0 = ±1. Hence ξ(x) ≠ 0.

5. (iv) Assume U is open.
   (⊇) Let x ∈ M.
   - x ∈ U by R.carrier_subset.
   - As in parent step 2, since {x} is Borel and x ∈ M, μ_R({x}) = ∫⁻_{{x}∩M} θ dH⁰ = ∫⁻_{{x}} θ dH⁰ = θ(x)·H⁰({x}) = θ(x) ≥ 1 (withDensity_apply, Measure.restrict_restrict, lintegral_singleton).
   - Every neighbourhood N of x contains {x}, so μ_R(N) ≥ 1 > 0. Hence x ∈ spt μ_R (Measure.mem_support_iff_forall), and M ⊆ U ∩ spt μ_R.
   (⊆) Let x ∈ U ∩ spt μ_R and suppose x ∉ M.
   - Choose ε > 0 with B_ε(x) ⊆ U, since U is open.
   - The closed ball B̄ := B̄_{ε/2}(x) ⊆ B_ε(x) ⊆ U is compact, since ℝ^P is proper. So F := M ∩ B̄ is finite by (ii), hence closed, and x ∉ F.
   - Choose δ > 0 with B_δ(x) ∩ F = ∅, and put η := min(δ, ε/2) > 0.
   - A point z ∈ B_η(x) ∩ M would lie both in B̄ ∩ M = F and in B_δ(x), which is impossible. So B_η(x) ∩ M = ∅.
   - B_η(x) is open, hence Borel, so μ_R(B_η(x)) = ∫⁻_{M∩B_η(x)} θ dH⁰ = 0.
   - But B_η(x) is a neighbourhood of x ∈ spt μ_R, so μ_R(B_η(x)) > 0 (Measure.mem_support_iff_forall), a contradiction.
   - Hence x ∈ M, and U ∩ spt μ_R = M. ∎
proof_key_steps: H⁰ = μH[0] gives every point mass 1, every nonempty set mass at least 1, and every finite set mass equal to its cardinality.
The H⁰-null set of the rectifiable cover is empty, and each image of the one-point space ℝ⁰ is at most a point, so M is countable.
Because θ ≥ 1 on M, H⁰(M∩K) ≤ ∫_{M∩K} θ dH⁰ = μ_R(K) < ∞ for compact K ⊆ U, so M ∩ K is finite.
Every carrier point has H⁰⌞M-mass 1, so the a.e. orientation property holds at every carrier point. ξ(x) sends the constant covector 1 to ±1, so ξ(x) ≠ 0.
For open U, carrier points have μ_R-mass θ(x) ≥ 1, and a point of U off M has a ball missing the locally finite set M, so U ∩ spt μ_R = M.

subproblems.title: A degree-0 unit orientation is ± evaluation at the empty tuple (reused accepted lemma)
subproblems.statement: Let P ∈ ℕ, let ξ ∈ MultiVector P 0 (a continuous linear functional on the 0-covectors of ℝ^P), and let Q be a subspace of ℝ^P with IsUnitOrientationOf ξ Q. Then there is s ∈ ℝ with |s| = 1 such that ξ(α) = s·α(⟨⟩) for every 0-covector α. Here ⟨⟩ = (fun i => i.elim0) : Fin 0 → ℝ^P is the empty tuple.
subproblems.lean_statement: ∀ (P : ℕ) (ξ : MultiVector P 0) (Q : Submodule ℝ (Euclid P)), IsUnitOrientationOf ξ Q → ∃ s : ℝ, |s| = 1 ∧ ∀ α : Covector (Euclid P) 0, ξ α = s * α (fun i => i.elim0)
subproblems.natural_proof:
Source: step 5 of the parent proof ("there are Q and an orthonormal τ : Fin 0 → ℝ^P with ζ(x)(α) = α(τ) for all α or ζ(x)(α) = −α(τ) for all α; as Fin 0 is empty, τ is the empty tuple ⟨⟩. Hence ζ(x)(α) = s(x)·α(⟨⟩) with s(x) ∈ {1, −1}"), stated for an arbitrary ξ and Q. In Simon 6.2.2 (chapter-06.txt lines 198–203) an orientation is ξ = ±τ₁ ∧ ⋯ ∧ τₙ; for n = 0 the empty wedge is 1. Notation: ⟨⟩ := (fun i => i.elim0) : Fin 0 → ℝ^P.

1. Unfold IsUnitOrientationOf ξ Q. There is τ : Fin 0 → ℝ^P (orthonormal, with span(range τ) = Q; these two properties are not used below) such that either
   (a) ξ(α) = α(τ) for every 0-covector α, or
   (b) ξ(α) = −α(τ) for every 0-covector α.
2. τ = ⟨⟩. Two functions Fin 0 → ℝ^P agree at every i : Fin 0 vacuously, because Fin 0 has no elements (Fin.elim0). So they are equal by function extensionality. Hence α(τ) = α(⟨⟩) for every 0-covector α.
3. In case (a) put s := 1. Then |s| = 1 and, for every α, ξ(α) = α(τ) = α(⟨⟩) = 1·α(⟨⟩) by step 2.
4. In case (b) put s := −1. Then |s| = |−1| = 1 and, for every α, ξ(α) = −α(τ) = −α(⟨⟩) = (−1)·α(⟨⟩) by step 2.
5. In either case |s| = 1 and ξ(α) = s·α(⟨⟩) for every 0-covector α. ∎
proof_key_steps: Unfold IsUnitOrientationOf to get τ : Fin 0 → ℝ^P with ξ(α) = α(τ) for all α, or ξ(α) = −α(τ) for all α.
Every function Fin 0 → ℝ^P equals the empty tuple ⟨⟩, so α(τ) = α(⟨⟩).
Take s = 1 in the first case and s = −1 in the second; in both cases |s| = 1.

subproblems.title: Integrals over finite sets against H⁰ are sums of values
subproblems.statement: Let P ∈ ℕ, let F be a finite subset of ℝ^P (a Finset), and let f : ℝ^P → ℝ be any function. Then ∫_F f dH⁰ = Σ_{x∈F} f(x). Here H⁰ = μHE[0], and the left side is the Bochner integral of f against H⁰ restricted to the set F.
subproblems.lean_statement: ∀ (P : ℕ) (F : Finset (Euclid P)) (f : Euclid P → ℝ), ∫ x in (F : Set (Euclid P)), f x ∂μHE[0] = ∑ x ∈ F, f x
subproblems.natural_proof:
Source: step 6 of the parent proof ("The integrand is integrable on the finite set M₀, each singleton having finite measure (integrableOn_singleton_iff, integrableOn_finset_iUnion), so ∫_{M₀} h dH⁰ = Σ_{x∈F} H⁰({x})·h(x) = Σ_{x∈F} h(x) (setIntegral_finset)"), together with step 1 (H⁰({x}) = 1). Both are stated here for an arbitrary finite set and an arbitrary real function. In Simon, H⁰ is counting measure (chapter-02.txt line 787). Write H⁰ = μHE[0].

1. Point masses.
   - H⁰ = μH[0] on ℝ^P (Measure.euclideanHausdorffMeasure_zero).
   - So H⁰({x}) = 1 for every x ∈ ℝ^P (Measure.hausdorffMeasure_zero_singleton).
   - In particular H⁰({x}) < ∞, and H⁰.real({x}) := (H⁰({x})).toReal = 1.
2. Integrability on a singleton. Fix x ∈ ℝ^P.
   - The restricted measure H⁰⌞{x} has total mass H⁰({x}) = 1, so it is finite. It gives zero mass to ℝ^P ∖ {x}.
   - Hence f agrees (H⁰⌞{x})-a.e. with the constant f(x).
   - A real constant is integrable against a finite measure, so f is integrable on {x}.
   - In Mathlib this is integrableOn_singleton. Its side conditions hold: ‖f(x)‖ₑ ≠ ∞ because f(x) is real, H⁰({x}) < ∞ by step 1, and ℝ^P has measurable singletons.
3. Integrability on F.
   - As sets, F = ⋃_{x∈F} {x}, a finite union.
   - A function integrable on each of finitely many sets is integrable on their union (integrableOn_finset_iUnion).
   - By step 2, f is therefore integrable on F against H⁰.
4. Evaluation. For a function integrable on a finite set, in a space with measurable singletons, setIntegral_finset gives ∫_F f dH⁰ = Σ_{x∈F} H⁰.real({x}) · f(x).
5. By step 1, H⁰.real({x}) = 1 for every x. So ∫_F f dH⁰ = Σ_{x∈F} 1·f(x) = Σ_{x∈F} f(x). ∎
proof_key_steps: μHE[0] = μH[0] gives every singleton H⁰-mass 1.
f is integrable on each singleton (finite measure, a.e. constant), hence on the finite union F.
setIntegral_finset gives ∫_F f dH⁰ = Σ H⁰.real({x})·f(x) = Σ_{x∈F} f(x).
